subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage: "Urmila, dinner!" "Not hungry." Darshan bhaiya leaned on her door. "You've changed your hair three times since March." "So?" "So nothing. Just asking. Last month it was the debate club, now it's the skateboard lot." "Can you not?" "I'm not having a go. I just want to know which Urmila I'm eating dinner with." She threw a cushion at him. "I don't know, okay? Every group feels like wearing someone else's clothes." Darshan came in and sat on the floor. "I did the same at your age. Cricket boys, then theatre, then nobody for a while." "Seriously?" "Seriously. Felt awful." Urmila picked at the cushion's tassel. "Did it stop?" "Slowly. Come and eat."

qa.q: Which club was Urmila in last month?
qa.a: The debate club.

qa.q: What does Urmila mean when she says every group feels like wearing someone else's clothes?
qa.a: She feels lost and out of place in every group, and it unsettles her that she can't say who she really is.

qa.q: What choice did Darshan make that helped Urmila open up?
qa.a: He stopped teasing, sat on her floor and shared that he went through the same thing, which made her feel less strange.

qa.q: What is it like for Darshan to watch Urmila change so often?
qa.a: Darshan is curious and a little worried, but remembers doing the same at her age, so he can be patient rather than annoyed.

grounding: A teenage girl who keeps switching groups and styles snaps at her brother, admits she doesn't know who she is, and hears it is a stage he went through too.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage: I'm Preeti, and this year I've been three different girls. In January I was the quiet one in the science group, nodding along about exams. By April I'd dyed a streak of my hair blue and sat with the art crowd, saying marks didn't matter. In June I joined the football girls and told everyone art was pointless. Vijay, who has known me since nursery, asked, "Which one's actually you?" I snapped at him and didn't speak to him for three days. The truth is I didn't know. At night I'd lie there feeling like a costume with nobody inside. Last week Mum told me she changed friends four times in Class 10. That helped a bit. I still don't have an answer for Vijay. Maybe I'm allowed not to, yet.

qa.q: What colour did Preeti dye a streak of hair in April?
qa.a: Blue.

qa.q: What does Preeti mean by feeling 'like a costume with nobody inside'?
qa.a: She feels empty and unsure, as if each group's style is something she wears without knowing who she is underneath.

qa.q: What was a turning point for Preeti, and what could she say to Vijay now?
qa.a: Hearing that Mum changed friends four times in Class 10; she could tell Vijay she doesn't know yet and apologise for snapping.

qa.q: How might Vijay have felt when Preeti snapped and stopped speaking for three days?
qa.a: Vijay probably felt hurt and confused, since the question came from a friend who has known her since nursery.

grounding: A teenage girl moves through three friend groups and opinions in months, snaps at a friend, feels empty, and begins to accept not knowing yet as normal.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage: Class teacher's note, Class 9B, 18 October. Written by Rafiq Sir. Jahnavi has changed a great deal since June. In the first term she sat with the quiz team and argued hard for every answer. In August she moved to the back benches with a new group, and her notebook filled up with song lyrics. Last week she told the class exams are useless, then asked me after the bell whether she could still join the quiz team next year. She has snapped at two friends and eaten lunch alone on some days. Her marks are steady. I don't see a problem to fix so much as a young person trying on different selves. I told her it is normal not to know yet, and that the quiz door is still open. I've asked her parents to keep things calm at home, and I will keep an eye on the lunches.

qa.q: What filled Jahnavi's notebook in August?
qa.a: Song lyrics.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi be feeling when she calls exams useless but asks about the quiz team?
qa.a: She seems unsure and pulled in different directions, trying out a new attitude while still wanting an old part of herself.

qa.q: What choice did Rafiq Sir make instead of treating the changes as a problem?
qa.a: He told Jahnavi it is normal not to know yet, kept the quiz door open, and asked her parents to keep things calm while he watched the lunches.

qa.q: How might the two friends she snapped at see Jahnavi right now?
qa.a: They may feel hurt or confused, not knowing she is struggling to work out who she is.

grounding: A teacher notes a girl moving between groups, styles and opinions, with irritability and some withdrawal, and treats it as a normal search for self.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage:
Friday
Sat with the hockey girls at lunch again. Two weeks ago I was with Jaya and the book club lot, and before that I wore only black and said I hated everyone. Jaya passed me in the corridor and said, "Which Uma is it today?" She was joking. I think.
I don't know which Uma it is. I like the hockey girls' noise, but I went quiet when they laughed at the book club. I cut my hair short last month and I keep touching it like it belongs to someone else.
Snapped at Amma at dinner when she asked why her girl was so quiet. A normal question. Went to my room. Didn't cry, just lay there.
Ms Thomas said in class that people our age try on selves like clothes. Maybe. It still feels weird.
Uma

qa.q: What did Jaya say in the corridor?
qa.a: Jaya said, 'Which Uma is it today?'

qa.q: How can you tell that Uma feels unsettled about who she is?
qa.a: She touches her short hair as if it belongs to someone else, went quiet when the book club was mocked, and snapped at Amma.

qa.q: What could Uma do after snapping at Amma?
qa.a: She could apologise and tell Amma she has been feeling mixed up lately, which would help Amma understand the moods.

qa.q: How might Jaya feel about Uma moving from the book club to the hockey girls?
qa.a: Jaya might feel a little hurt or confused, which could be behind the half-joke in the corridor.

grounding: A teenager's diary shows her moving between friend groups and looks, unsure who she is, irritable at home, and told this is a normal part of growing.

subtopic: Identity foreclosure, moratorium and role confusion
passage:
Bhavna: bhaiya can I ask something weird
Kunal: always
Bhavna: how did you know what kind of person you were
Kunal: I didn't. still don't fully
Bhavna: I've changed friend groups twice since the summer holidays. now I'm in the drama gang. last month I was with the coding kids saying drama was cringe
Bhavna: yesterday I argued FOR something I argued against in july
Bhavna: I don't even know what I actually think
Kunal: that sounds tiring
Bhavna: it is. and I keep being rude to mummy and I don't know why
Kunal: honestly at 15 I switched groups like four times. it's kind of how you figure it out
Bhavna: so I'm not fake
Kunal: no. you're trying things on. maybe just tell mummy you're a bit all over the place, not angry at her
Bhavna: ok 🙂

qa.q: What did Bhavna say about drama last month?
qa.a: Last month Bhavna was with the coding kids saying drama was cringe.

qa.q: What is Bhavna worried about when asking 'so I'm not fake'?
qa.a: Bhavna worries that switching groups and opinions means being fake, and feels confused about what they actually think.

qa.q: What small step does Kunal suggest, and why is it useful?
qa.a: Telling Mummy that Bhavna is a bit all over the place, not angry at her, so the rudeness isn't taken personally.

qa.q: How might Mummy experience Bhavna's rudeness if she doesn't know what's going on?
qa.a: She might feel hurt or puzzled, taking the snapping personally when it really comes from Bhavna's confusion.

grounding: A teenager tells Kunal, whom they call bhaiya, about switching groups and opinions and not knowing what they think, and learns this is a normal part of finding a self.
